sections.authorBiography: Nathaniel Hawthorne was born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 4 July 1804; his ancestor John Hathorne was a judge in the Salem witch trials of 1692, a family history Hawthorne felt as a burden (he added the "w" to his name). After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 he spent years writing in near-seclusion in Salem, publishing Twice-Told Tales in 1837. He lived briefly at the utopian Brook Farm community, worked at the Salem Custom House, and achieved fame with The Scarlet Letter (1850) and The House of the Seven Gables (1851). He served as U.S. consul in Liverpool and died on 19 May 1864 in Plymouth, New Hampshire.
sections.historicalContext: The story is set in Salem village in Puritan New England, around the end of the seventeenth century, the world of the 1692 witch trials. Hawthorne's great-great-grandfather John Hathorne was a judge at those trials, and Hawthorne added the "w" to his name partly to distance himself from that inheritance. Puritans believed in human depravity and watched one another for signs of sin.

publicationAndReception.publication: First published anonymously in the New-England Magazine in April 1835; collected in Mosses from an Old Manse (1846).
publicationAndReception.then: Little noticed at first; Herman Melville praised the story warmly in his 1850 essay "Hawthorne and His Mosses."
publicationAndReception.now: A central text of American Romanticism and "dark romanticism," studied for its allegory and its deliberate ambiguity.

sections.overview: A young Puritan husband leaves his new wife, Faith, for one night to keep a mysterious appointment in the forest with a traveller who carries a serpent-like staff.

not knowing the truth destroys him.

sections.whyItMatters: The story asks what happens when we see evil in everyone, and how suspicion poisons a community, from 1692 Salem to modern rumour.

spoilerOverview.text: In the forest he sees the town's most respected people, and apparently Faith, gathering for a witches' meeting; he calls on her to resist and wakes alone. Whether it was a dream or not, he lives the rest of his life gloomy and distrustful, and dies without hope.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Young Goodman Brown.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Young Goodman Brown: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

items.prompt: What is the name of Brown's wife?

options: A staff that looks like a twisting serpent

items.prompt: Whom does Brown see in the forest?
What does Brown find on a branch?
options: A pink ribbon from Faith's cap

items.prompt: How does Brown live after that night?
options: Stern, sad and distrustful until death

items.prompt: In the line “considerably nettled, "there is my wife, Faith.”, what does “nettled” most nearly mean?
options: in a self-collected or self-possessed manner

items.prompt: In the line “Though their figures brushed the small boughs by the wayside, it could not be seen that they intercepted, even for a moment, the faint gleam from the strip of bright sky athwart which they must have passed.”, what does “intercepted” most nearly mean?
options: in a self-collected or self-possessed manner

items.prompt: As used in the story (“considerably nettled, "there is my wife, Faith.”), what does “nettled” mean?
As used in the story (“Though their figures brushed the small boughs by the wayside, it could not be seen that they intercepted, even for a moment, the faint gleam”), what does “intercepted” mean?
As used in the story (“They continued to walk onward, while the elder traveller exhorted his companion to make good speed and persevere in the path, discoursing so”), what does “auditor” mean?
options: bend one's back forward from the waist on down
to a great extent or degree
in a self-collected or self-possessed manner

items.prompt: As used in the story (“composedly. "Sit here and rest yourself a while; and when you”), what does “composedly” mean?
options: in a self-collected or self-possessed manner

items.prompt: As used in the story (“The good old minister was taking a walk along the graveyard to get an appetite for breakfast and meditate his sermon, and bestowed a blessin”), what does “meditate” mean?

wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (faith and doubt, hypocrisy, the nature of evil) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Young Goodman Brown teaches about faith and doubt. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Nathaniel Hawthorne develops faith and doubt in Young Goodman Brown. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Nathaniel Hawthorne develops faith and doubt across Young Goodman Brown. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Young Goodman Brown (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of faith and doubt. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of faith and doubt in Young Goodman Brown. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Nathaniel Hawthorne's choices in Young Goodman Brown (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of faith and doubt, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Young Goodman Brown's treatment of faith and doubt in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on faith and doubt in Young Goodman Brown that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on faith and doubt in Young Goodman Brown. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about faith and doubt in Young Goodman Brown, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on faith and doubt in Young Goodman Brown, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
